proposal.lab.course.oneholetable.for: a search needs anchors, and six of the seven courses have none
proposal.lab.course.oneholetable.text: Of the seven course manifests only DashsTrack carries a per-hole sourceBox table; the others name an image, aliases and sweep cases. The port refuses a course with no viewport table the way `lab scope hN` does, and searches a second manifest it owns.

proposal.lab.exec.carriedtheport.for: what the studio core already had that the LAB needed
proposal.lab.exec.carriedtheport.text: readPql takes its parser explicitly, so the LAB's YAML ran unedited once a 120-line reader existed. classifyTick's chain rule is the LAB's own rule (every S1 Tick is a chain: selectHsvMask -> group8Connected, and the five-Calculation BadgeAssembly). Multi-`into` carried the search Tick that publishes the next search state and the path in one pass.

proposal.lab.fixture.statedbasis.for: a synthetic fixture with no stated basis can be tuned until the Stage passes
proposal.lab.fixture.statedbasis.text: Every Stage here is checked against a capture this port drew. That is only honest if the capture says what each element answers to, so `fixtureBasis()` is a Part: the background values are chosen to fall outside both S1 masks (never <= 45, never >= 210), the badge geometry is the plate knobs, the basket is the LAB sprite inside a 4px shell, the tee is the elongated enclosed hole, and the obstacle is drawn outside every S1/S2/S3 predicate on purpose so that no Stage object can own it.
proposal.lab.fixture.statedbasis.proposal: one corpus capture would replace the whole argument with a value oracle (proposal.lab.oracle.nocorpus).

proposal.lab.holes.nearestisafallback.for: why the first rule this port invented for assembling a hole is kept but not numbered
proposal.lab.holes.nearestisafallback.text: The nearest-free-anchor binding was built as "S4" and then superseded on the same day: the owner's numbering makes S4 recovery, S5 the tee-to-badge ray (a tee POINTS at its badge), S6 the straight holes (three points make a line, so the basket is on the ray beyond the badge) and S7 pathfinding. The difference is not a refinement, it is a different kind of claim: nearest-anchor is a guess that is always available, the ray is evidence the picture actually carries and is sometimes absent. So the fallback keeps its Stage shape and its invariants under the name HolesByNearestAnchor, unnumbered, and the two rules disagreeing on a hole is a thing a reader can see rather than a thing that never happens.
proposal.lab.holes.nearestisafallback.proposal: when both run, publish the disagreement as its own Part: a hole the ray resolved one way and the distance another is the most interesting object on the course.

proposal.lab.oracle.nocorpus.for: an oracle is what turns a port into a proof
proposal.lab.oracle.nocorpus.text: Nothing in the LAB records an expected value this port could check against: S0 and S1 read a corpus image that is not in this repository, and the Mermaid experiment is explicitly unrun ("compilation, tests, execution and rendering await review"). The port is checked by structure (compiled document equals the YAML by digest), by the LAB's own invariants (owned, muted and remaining partition the raster) and by a fixture built to the LAB's knobs.
proposal.lab.oracle.nocorpus.workaround: a deterministic synthetic capture whose badges are drawn to the plate/border/digit geometry the S1 knobs accept.
proposal.lab.oracle.nocorpus.proposal: ask for one corpus image and one recorded S1 run; both paths then compare value by value the way proof.ts does.

proposal.lab.pql.directresult.for: a Stage whose point is that a big intermediate is never published cannot be ported without publishing it
proposal.lab.pql.directresult.text: The LAB's Mermaid compiler binds a Calculation's result directly: `with: { image: { kind: 'fn', ref: 'decode' } }`. S0's FullImage is never a Part, and the LAB's proof checks exactly that (compare.ts `fullImageLocal`, proof.ts `!generated.pxc.has('px.source.fullImage')`). The studio's PQL binds addresses only.
proposal.lab.pql.directresult.workaround: lowerToPql mints one address per unpublished result (px.exp.lab.s0.local.decode) and reports it.
proposal.lab.pql.directresult.proposal: a binding kind that names a sibling Calculation in the same Tick, or a Part the record marks Tick-local.

proposal.lab.pql.effecttick.for: S0's third Tick exists to write a cache, and the grammar has no way to say so
proposal.lab.pql.effecttick.text: The LAB's S0_CACHE_TICK declares `produces: []`. The studio's readPql refuses it: 'a Calculation that publishes nothing has no place in this grammar'.
proposal.lab.pql.effecttick.workaround: fn.lab.s0.cachefullimage publishes a cache receipt Part instead.
proposal.lab.pql.effecttick.proposal: allow an empty `into` for a Calculation whose effect the receipt records, the way pyto marks oc. Calculations.

proposal.lab.pql.fanout.for: a Stage that computes one object per member of a family cannot say so in a document
proposal.lab.pql.fanout.text: The LAB's S2 Tick `Basket.findPx` invokes `fn.Basket.findPx` once per shell member inside one Tick, and its receipt lists every invocation. A PQL document names a Calculation once, with one `into`, so the port's Calculation maps over the members and publishes the array.
proposal.lab.pql.fanout.workaround: fn.lab.basket.findpx takes the whole shell family and returns the Basket objects.
proposal.lab.pql.fanout.proposal: a Calculation that fans out over a collection input, each invocation its own line in the receipt.

proposal.lab.pql.occurrenceid.for: comparing two runs Calculation by Calculation needs a name that survives an edit
proposal.lab.pql.occurrenceid.text: The Mermaid compiler gives every Calculation the graph's node id, and the LAB's runner names values and failures by it ('failed at decode'). PQL gives a Calculation no id; exec.js names it by position, call and into.
proposal.lab.pql.occurrenceid.workaround: the port compares by position, which is what proof.ts does too.
proposal.lab.pql.occurrenceid.proposal: an optional `id` on a Calculation, carried into the receipt and the run record.

proposal.lab.route.objectivefromstages.for: what pathfinding means once the Stages have run
proposal.lab.route.objectivefromstages.text: The hex walk had to invent an objective because the LAB has none. The Stages give one: S1 reads the hole numbers, S2 finds the baskets, S3 the visible tees, so a path is the round itself -- each hole tee to basket in badge order, then basket to the next tee. The anchors come from the produce Parts, not from the course manifest, and the fixture proves the order is the reading and not the raster position (badge "01" is played before badge "10", which sits higher in the image).

proposal.lab.route.straightlegs.for: a round is measured today, not routed
proposal.lab.route.straightlegs.text: The legs are straight lines between anchors. The Stages already publish the obstacle information a real leg would respect (px.remaining.afterBadges, and the exact Basket and Tee pixels), and nothing consumes it yet.
proposal.lab.route.straightlegs.workaround: the leg carries its length and refuses an anchor outside the canonical raster.
proposal.lab.route.straightlegs.proposal: a Route Tick that reads px.remaining.afterBadges as cost and searches it, with the hex walk as its move set.

proposal.lab.s1.recognition.for: the one Calculation of S1 that is reduced rather than ported
proposal.lab.s1.recognition.text: fn.s1.whiteDigits.prepare/match segment glyphs with knobs and score them with a logistic model asset (digits/logisticInference, assets/logistic.json). The port normalizes to the same digitW x digitH grid and scores against template Parts; the reading shape (value, status, per-digit rankings) is the LAB's.

proposal.lab.s3.badgemute.for: why the Stages have to run in order
proposal.lab.s3.badgemute.text: S3's fixture finds four enclosed holes: two tee glyphs and two badge digit holes. The two digit holes are removed by S1's Badge mute footprint, which is the only reason S3's family vote sees a clean pair. Run S3 without S1 and the same detector produces a different family: the order S0 -> S1 -> S2 -> S3 is load-bearing, not administrative.

proposal.lab.s3.pythonoracle.for: an oracle for a Stage with no recorded values
proposal.lab.s3.pythonoracle.text: The Python analogue (experiments/quick-anno-python/s3.py at 6309ff1) is an accounting PCR over S3's own output: enclosed = elongated + diamondDropped, elongated = candidates + excludedByBadge, candidates = measured + unframed, measured = familyMembers + votedOutOfFamily, familyMembers = tees. The port runs it as its own two-Tick composition (the second Tick consuming the first's published Part, the shape S3_CHECKPOINT.md describes) and the balance holds on the fixture.

proposal.lab.s4.everyoverlapbreaksonepre.for: what an overlap actually does to a detector
proposal.lab.s4.everyoverlapbreaksonepre.text: Each clean detector has one thing it cannot survive, and it is not noise -- it is a predicate. S1 needs a white component whose bbox encloses the plate, so cutting the border ring twice loses the badge while leaving the plate untouched. S2 needs the body component to be the sprite's bbox EXACTLY, so a 10x4 white tab fused to it loses the basket while leaving the shell untouched. S3 needs an enclosed hole, and it dilates by up to 3 to close gaps, so a notch 10px wide loses the tee while leaving the frame's bbox untouched. In all three the object's other half is still there, which is why recovery is possible at all and why each rule reads the half the overlap did not touch.

proposal.lab.s4.missingisnotaguess.for: the one thing a hole assembler must never do
proposal.lab.s4.missingisnotaguess.text: Hole 11 of the course fixture has a badge and a tee and no basket, because the fixture draws no third basket. S4 reports `basket: null`, `missing: ['basket']`, confidence 0.75 out of a stated sum, and lists the hole under `px.holes.unplaced.incomplete` with the reason. The alternative every nearest-neighbour binder reaches for -- take the nearest basket even though another hole already has it, or interpolate one -- is refused by two invariants at once (`everyBasketOnce` and `missingIsNotGuessed`), and the test proves both refuse it.
proposal.lab.s4.missingisnotaguess.proposal: a recovery Tick could look for a basket S2 missed, but it would publish a candidate with its own confidence, not fill this field.

proposal.lab.s4.recoveryisadd-only.for: the rule that makes recovery safe rather than generous
proposal.lab.s4.recoveryisadd-only.text: Recovery searches only px.recovered.unclaimed -- the components of either mask that no clean Badge, Basket or Tee owns a pixel of -- so it cannot take an object away from a Stage, move one, or disagree with one. It only adds, only where the clean path found nothing, and every object it adds carries the rule that found it (`basis`) and the measurement that admitted it (`evidence`). Two invariants hold the line: everyCleanObjectSurvivesUnchanged compares against the raw S1/S2/S3 Parts rather than S4's copy of them, and noRecoveredObjectSitsOnACleanOne refuses an object on top of one that was already found.

proposal.lab.s4.ruleliftedintoastage.for: what changes when a rule stops being a step of a search and becomes a Stage
proposal.lab.s4.ruleliftedintoastage.text: The straight route (task 114) binds each hole to the nearest free tee and basket inside its Order Tick. S4 is that same rule with nothing else around it, and the difference is that it can now be checked: the binding publishes its pools (every anchor with the hole that took it), so `everyTeeOnce`, `everyBasketOnce` and `everyBadgeOnce` are arithmetic over a published Part rather than a property of a function nobody can see into. The rule did not get better; it got inspectable, which is what a Tick boundary is for.

proposal.lab.s4.thelabhadonerecoveryandn.for: where the three recovery rules came from
proposal.lab.s4.thelabhadonerecoveryandn.text: S1 has a recovery and it is implemented: recoverDarkPlateBadges finds a badge whose bright border never formed, from the dark plate alone, and the object records basis 'dark-plate-recovery' beside 'bright-family' and 'unresolved'. S2's and S3's receipts NAME two more and run neither: 'recovery: NOT RUN' (S2/contract.ts:19) and 'recovery: NOT RUN' / 'component fallback: NOT RUN' (S3/contract.ts:25-26). So the port did not invent a scheme; it ported the one that exists and wrote the two the LAB had already given names to, in the same shape: a shell that survives the body it holds, and a frame that is still a frame after its hole leaks.

proposal.lab.s5.blockedbeforerouted.for: what a course can say before anything searches it
proposal.lab.s5.blockedbeforerouted.text: S5's edges carry `straightIsBlocked`, sampled at half a cell along the straight line between anchors. On the course fixture two of the three edges are blocked -- the walk from basket-2 back to tee-2 and the play of hole 10 -- which is the whole of S6's problem stated before S6 exists, and the reason the S6 landing can be compared against the straight route rather than merely admired.

proposal.lab.s5.directionisameasurement.for: the difference between an axis and a direction
proposal.lab.s5.directionisameasurement.text: A tee's major axis (the LAB's own majorAxisOf, already in the component stats S2 publishes) gives a line and two ends, and nothing about an axis says which end is the front. S5 measures it: the centroid of the pad's bright material against the centre of the RING S3 detected -- the one landmark a nose does not move -- and takes the end the material leans toward, provided it leans at least half a pixel. A pad balanced about its own ring has no front and is reported that way. The bbox centre will NOT do as the reference: a nose grows the bbox by about as much as it shifts the material, and on the fixture the two cancel to 0.045px, which is how the first version of this Stage came out pointing at nothing.

proposal.lab.s5.terrainisaresidue.for: where an obstacle map comes from when no Stage was ever asked to find obstacles
proposal.lab.s5.terrainisaresidue.text: S5 detects nothing. It classifies every pixel of the canonical raster by which Stage already owns it -- badge (not in px.remaining.afterBadges), basket, tee -- and calls what is left over AND still dark in S1's own black mask `terrain`. On the course fixture that is exactly the 4224 pixels of the drawn bar and not one pixel more, because every basket and tee pixel leaves through its own door first. An obstacle map is a residue of the Stages, and the Stage that produces it is the one that says every pixel leaves once.

proposal.lab.s5.walkablerulestated.for: the one judgement in S5 that the raster cannot settle
proposal.lab.s5.walkablerulestated.text: Four of the five classes are printed on a map: a badge, a basket and a tee are symbols, and a tee or a basket is where a leg ENDS, so making them obstacles would make every leg unreachable. Only terrain blocks. That is a choice about what the picture means, not a fact about the pixels, so it is carried in the Part (`px.course.graph.walkableRule`) rather than buried in a predicate.
proposal.lab.s5.walkablerulestated.proposal: a real course would classify terrain further (water, trees, out of bounds) and give each class a cost instead of a boolean; the cell grid already has the shape for it.

proposal.lab.s6.determinismisdesigned.for: a search that has to give the same answer on two machines
proposal.lab.s6.determinismisdesigned.text: Integer step costs (10 orthogonal, 14 diagonal) and an octile heuristic in the same units mean no float ever decides an ordering; the frontier is chosen by (f, g, cell index), which is a total order, and the eight moves are visited in a fixed order. No clock, no random, no Map insertion order. Two independent runs of the whole Stage produce the same cells, the same cost and the same length, which is the test.

proposal.lab.s6.doglegsarethework.for: what the straight-hole rule leaves for whoever comes next
proposal.lab.s6.doglegsarethework.text: px.holes.unresolved is not an error list. It carries, per badge, the reason the straight rule could not finish it (no tee points at it, the ray left the raster, the basket found was off the line, or the basket was already taken), plus the tees and baskets left over. That is the exact inheritance of a stage that can follow a bend: which badges, which anchors, and what was already ruled out.

proposal.lab.s6.gridoverhead.for: what a cell path costs even when nothing is in the way
proposal.lab.s6.gridoverhead.text: The leg that nothing blocks (hole 1, tee-3 to basket-2) still comes out 6.7% longer than its straight line, because the path is a sequence of cell centres at 16px and an A* on a grid can only move in eight directions. That is not the obstacle map costing anything; it is the discretisation. It is reported per leg as `detourRatio` rather than smoothed away, so a reader can tell the two costs apart.
proposal.lab.s6.gridoverhead.proposal: a line-of-sight pass (string pulling) over the cells would return the straight line where the straight line is walkable, and only bend where it is not.

proposal.lab.s6.themapiswhatchanged.for: what the straight route got wrong, measured rather than asserted
proposal.lab.s6.themapiswhatchanged.text: The straight route (task 114) and S6 bind the same holes to the same tees and baskets in the same order -- `sameHoles` and `sameAnchors` in px.exp.lab.s6.vsstraight are both true. The straight route was never wrong about WHERE the round goes; it was wrong about the ground in between: two of its three legs pass through four obstacle cells, and on the course fixture respecting the map costs 316.2 px on 1170.4 (+27%), almost all of it on one play leg (+72%). That is the whole difference between a round that is measured and a round that is walked.

proposal.lab.s6.theresidualiswhatmakesit.for: why a ray beats a nearest-basket rule even when they agree
proposal.lab.s6.theresidualiswhatmakesit.text: Continuing the tee-to-badge ray gives the basket AND a number that can refute it: the perpendicular distance from the basket centre to the ray. On the fixture's aligned hole that residual is 0.5px. A nearest-basket rule produces an answer for every badge and no number at all; this produces an answer only where three points really are on a line, and says `this hole bends` everywhere else. Two of the fixture's three badges come out as doglegs, which is the correct answer for a course drawn with tees that do not point.

proposal.lab.s6.unreachableisaresult.for: the answer a search must be allowed to give
proposal.lab.s6.unreachableisaresult.text: A basket with no walkable path to it makes a leg with `reachable: false`, no cells, no length, the reason, and the count of cells the search did reach; the round carries it under `unreachable` and its length excludes it. The invariant `unreachableIsReportedNotStraightened` refuses the alternative -- a straight line drawn across the thing that blocked it -- and the test builds a sealed room to prove the refusal fires.

proposal.lab.s7.playsonlywhatwasresolved.for: what a round may be played over
proposal.lab.s7.playsonlywhatwasresolved.text: S7's course graph binds px.holes.straight -- the holes whose tee, badge and basket S6 put on one line, each carrying its residual -- and takes px.holes.unresolved as `unplayed`. The nearest-anchor fallback still exists and still produces a hole for every badge, so the two rounds can be run side by side, and on the course fixture they are NOT the same course: the fallback plays hole 10 (its badge is a dogleg, bound to whatever tee and basket happened to be nearest) and S7 does not. `everyDoglegIsNamedNotRouted` refuses a course that quietly plays one.
proposal.lab.s7.playsonlywhatwasresolved.proposal: a stage that follows a bend would hand S7 more holes through the same binding; nothing else in S7 would change.

proposal.lab.s7.twokindsofdifference.for: why the comparison with the straight route had to be re-read after the rebase
proposal.lab.s7.twokindsofdifference.text: It used to measure one thing -- what going round an obstacle costs -- because both rounds played the same holes. Now it measures two, and says so: `divergence` names the holes each round plays and which the fallback played alone, and the two totals (`straightTotalPx`, `routedTotalPx`) are both over S7's OWN legs, with the fallback's whole round kept apart as `straight.wholeRoundLengthPx`. On the course fixture the ground costs +53.0px on 987.8 (+5.4%), of which one blocked play leg is +25.7 (+9.9%) and the rest is the cell grid; the fallback's round is a different 1562.0px over a different set of holes, and adding those two numbers together would have been meaningless.

proposal.lab.search.noobjective.for: what pathfinding means in the LAB before anyone writes a search
proposal.lab.search.noobjective.text: `lab traverse` renders the current point and its six hex neighbours (270/330/30/90/150/210 at one radius) and an agent picks one; `lab search` keeps trails, pins, pages and an event log. There is no objective function and no expansion: the search is the eye in the loop. The port keeps the geometry exactly and names the objective (fewest hex moves to within tolerance of a target anchor, inside the raster), so a path becomes a produce with a receipt and replays as `lab traverse move <n>` commands.
proposal.lab.search.noobjective.proposal: if the LAB wants an automatic search, the objective belongs in the course manifest beside the blind viewport.

proposal.lab.stage.inventedinthelabgramm.for: whether the LAB's stage grammar carries a Stage it never wrote
proposal.lab.stage.inventedinthelabgramm.text: S4, S5 and S6 are not ports: nothing in ChainSpot corresponds to them. They were written in the LAB's own grammar anyway -- a contract naming consumes and produces, Ticks whose names are the OperationSpecs, one published Part per Calculation, a `has` provenance block on each constructed object, an accounting PCR as the oracle where no reference run exists, and a .mmd that compiles to the same document. Every one of those fitted without being bent. The one thing the grammar did not carry is the choice S5 had to make about what an obstacle IS, which is why that choice is a field in the Part rather than a predicate in the code.

proposal.lab.stage.s0hasnopql.for: knowing which LAB documents are compositions and which are descriptions
proposal.lab.stage.s0hasnopql.text: S0 has no PQL document in ChainSpot: S0.pcr.yaml is a description (input / sanitation / transform / output / last / receipt) and the composition is three OperationSpecs executed by the gateway. The only PQL documents on this tip are S1/exp/badge-assembly/PrincipleComponentRender.yaml and what the Mermaid compiler emits. The port therefore compiles S0.mmd and appends the cache Tick the description names last.

proposal.lab.stage.specsaredocuments.for: porting a Stage that has no YAML
proposal.lab.stage.specsaredocuments.text: S2's composition is three OperationSpecs, each declaring consumes, produces and its one Calculation. That is a PQL document in another notation: the port writes it out (four Ticks with the substrate publish in front) and runs it unchanged. The same move works for S0; only S1 keeps a written PQL document.

px.exp.lab.course.obstacles.priority: a cell takes the first class present in it, in the order above

px.exp.lab.fixture.basis.for: why every element of the synthetic capture is drawn the way it is, and which Stage knob it answers to

frame.background: seeded LCG, values 80..199: never <= 45 (S1 black) and never >= 210 (S1 white), so every mask pixel below is drawn on purpose

elements.basis: constant rows top and bottom, no entropy: what S0 crops
S1's plate knobs (width 34..78, height 24..54, aspect 1..2.4, fill >= 0.55) and the digit templates the port carries in place of the LAB logistic asset
the LAB's own basket sprite (42x66, 1746 white px) inside a dark shell clearing it by 4px on every side: S2 learns that modal margin
a bright 16x26 outline 2px thick whose enclosed hole is small and elongated: S3 floods the background in and keeps what is enclosed

elements.what: the third badge "11" and third tee, with no third basket
elements.basis: S4 has to report a hole whose basket is missing instead of binding a basket that belongs to another hole; both digits are bars, so this badge adds no enclosed loop for S3 to mute

elements.what: the aligned hole: a pointing tee, its badge and its basket on one line
elements.basis: the tee carries a 6x4 bright nose on one short end, which is the only thing in the shape that tells its two ends apart, and the badge centre and the basket centre both sit on x=248, the tee's own major axis: S5 reads the pointing end off the pixels and S6 continues the ray past the badge to the basket. The other tees have no nose, so their rays are refused rather than guessed, and their badges are S6's doglegs

elements.what: the second aligned hole: another pointing tee and another basket, on the fixture's own "01" badge line
elements.basis: a pointing tee at (322,540) and a basket at (309,700), both centred on x=330, which is the centre of the badge already drawn at (300,620): a second straight hole, so a round has a leg to WALK between holes and not only a hole to play. The obstacle crosses the first hole's play line and not this one

one object per clean detector is occluded in the one way that detector cannot survive -- a cut border (S1 needs a white component enclosing the plate), a fused body (S2 needs the sprite bbox exactly), a notched frame (S3 needs an enclosed hole) -- and in each case the evidence the OTHER half of the object carries is left untouched, which is what S4 recovers from
264x16 at (0,380) in source coordinates: dark like a plate but outside every S1/S2/S3 predicate, so it is the one thing in the raster no Stage object owns and S5 can only call terrain

px.exp.lab.fixture.basis.seededBy: lcg(seed), no clock and no Math.random: the same bytes on every machine

px.exp.lab.holes.numbers.rule: badge order is the reading, not the position in the raster

px.exp.lab.holes.rayhits.rule: the tee-to-badge ray, continued past the badge; the first basket it enters is the hole basket

Recover.unclaimed -> Recover.badges -> Recover.baskets -> Recover.tees -> Recover.ledger: the LAB's own dark-plate recovery ported knob for knob, plus the shell recovery and component fallback its S2 and S3 receipts mark NOT RUN; px.recovered.* is what S5 onward read
Tee.pointing -> Tee.castRay -> TeeBadge.pair: the pointing end read off the pad's own bright material about its ring, then a ray; a symmetric pad is refused rather than paired by distance

stubbed.why: the LAB matches digits with a logistic model asset fitted on a corpus this repository does not have; the port normalizes the same way and matches template Parts built from the fixture's own glyph shapes

no recorded LAB values to check against: S0/S1 read chainspot-corpus/dev/DashsTrack/DashsTrack-full.jpg, absent here, and the Mermaid experiment records no generated output ("no generated output from this revision exists yet")
a route needs Stage outputs, and the Stages need a capture: the only capture here is the fixture, so DashsTrack is routed by the manifest hex walk and not by its own badges, baskets and tees

the three recovery rules are proved on three overlaps this port drew on purpose, each breaking exactly one clean predicate. A photograph overlaps objects in ways nobody designed, and the knobs that accept a recovery (plate glyph fraction, exact shell geometry, family fill) would meet cases the fixture cannot produce: a shell that is itself cut, a plate half off the frame, two tees fused into one component
the round is searched over the fixture, the only capture this repository has; on a real capture the obstacle map would be a photograph of trees and water rather than one bar drawn to be unclaimable

a leg is the cell path A* found, so an unobstructed leg still costs about 7% more than its straight line; a line-of-sight pass over the cells (string pulling) would remove that, and it is not written -- the number is reported in px.exp.lab.s6.vsstraight instead of being hidden

every walkable cell costs the same. A real course map distinguishes fairway, rough, water and out of bounds, and the grid already has the shape for a cost per cell; nothing here can tell those apart, so nothing here pretends to
the LAB anchors T/N/B come from the annotation truth file, which needs the corpus; the port searches the blind per-hole viewport the manifest itself carries
